newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Brussels readies for march over child sex scandal.
newsitem.headline: Brussels readies for march over child sex scandal.

text.p: Tens of thousands of demonstrators from Belgium and neighbouring countries streamed into Brussels under leaden skies on Sunday to march against a legal system that failed to stop a deadly paedophile ring.
Carrying white balloons and flowers, and some wearing white as a symbol of support for the victims of the ring, the marchers were gathering for a rally due to start at 2:00 p.m. (1200 GMT).

Protesters began to gather at the city's North Station with appeals for calm from King Albert, Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene and the parents of missing children and the victims ringing in their ears.

Some 1,400 police were on duty to ensure the safety of the estimated 100,000 people -- many of them children -- expected to take part in the demonstration, likely to be one of the largest in Belgium's history.

One of the marchers, Gerda Zammattio from the town of Mechelen with three-year-old Naomi, said, "I am here to show solidarity with the parents. What has happened in the last few weeks moved me greatly. The system must become more humane."
One Dutch-language banner read, "Ashamed to be Belgian."
Flemish marchers, part of a crowd of all ages and all walks of life, wore stickers across their foreheads saying, "Stop the cover-up."

Belgian railways pre-sold 64,000 subsidised return tickets to the demonstration and laid on almost 30 extra trains. Coaches have also been booked all over the country, while free parking and free bus and metro services are being provided in Brussels.

The march, not only aimed at what is seen as an incompetent law and order system, but also to show general dissatisfaction with the political class, is part of a groundswell of public emotion that one government minister said must be heeded.
At the heart of the rally is a national need to express sympathy with the victims of a gang alleged to have been led by convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux.
Dutroux, one of 13 people so far charged in connection with the case, was released 10 years early in 1992 from a 13-year sentence for multiple child rape.
But there is also concern about cover-ups in the inquiry into the sexual abuse and murder of four girls -- two were starved to death -- and the sexual abuse of at least two others by the gang.

The rally is an initiative by the parents of the dead children -- Julie Lejeune, Melissa Russo, Eefje Lambrecks and An Marchal -- and those of two missing girls -- Elisabeth Brichet and Loubna Benaissa.
The "White March" follows a week of protests that broke out spontaneously after Belgium's top court removed a popular magistrate from investigations into the ring.

The Cour de Cassation ruled that magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte had compromised himself by accepting a free dinner from the Marc et Corine group that specialises in helping the parents of missing children.

The ruling, following the letter rather than the spirit of the law, prompted an already morally-outraged public to take to the streets amid widespread allegations of a looming high-level cover-up and call for a radical clean-up of a justice system seen as corrupt.
The march was planned before Connerotte's dismissal, but has gained momentum since.
Workers at national airline Sabena, carrying white armbands, stopped work for five minutes on Sunday morning in support of the march and were due to do so again in the afternoon.
